newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's Van Miert urges worldwide competition rules.
newsitem.headline: EU's Van Miert urges worldwide competition rules.

text.p: European Union Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert on Monday launched a fervent appeal for international competition rules, saying trading partners such as Japan must play a role in fighting unfair practices.

"One of the reasons why the Japanese economy is not so open is because they do not have a competition policy like we and the United States have," Van Miert told a seminar organised by a Brussels think-tank, the Centre for European Policy Studies.

"Countries that have a competition policy or authority are ipso facto opening their markets," he added, singling out the case of the European telecommunications sector which is set for full liberalisation by January 1, 1998.

The European Commission -- the EU's executive -- has taken the lead in calling for international competition rules, possibly within the World Trade Organisation, but the move has little support from the United States, Van Miert said.
The Commission says rules are needed to cope with increasingly global markets and worldwide corporate alliances such as in the telecoms and media sectors.

"There are international cartels in the field of exportation," he said. Van Miert did not elaborate but the Commission has been trying for years to obtain changes to a price-sharing agreement, called the Trans-Atlantic Conference Agreenment, between large shipping companies on the transport of containers betwen the EU and the U.S.

In June it adopted a report, under the authority of Trade Commisioner Sir Leon Brittan and Van Miert, suggesting that a WTO working group should establish such rules or guidelines leaving its implementation to national competition authorities.
Van Miert said this could be accompanied by a dispute settlement within the WTO.

The Commission can already co-operate with the U.S. anti-trust authorities on cases involving alliances or practices affecting both markets in the framework of a competition agreement between the two sides of the Atlantic.
The agreements allows for consultation and the exchange of information on international mergers and marketing practices with the exception of confidential business information.
Past attempts to strike a similar deal with Japan has met with the resistance from Tokyo, Van Miert said.
